reading.rtitle: Opinion -- Sustainability Is Not a Cost
paras: THE PROBLEM. In my view, sustainability is the biggest topic in the coffee trade today. Two years ago, a long drought hit the region where many of our growers work. Because of the drought, the yield on many farms fell by a third, and prices went up all over the world. Many smallholders lost money, and some of them stopped producing coffee.

THE PRESSURE. At the same time, buyers in Europe are asking new questions. A new regulation says that coffee sold in the European Union must not come from land with recent deforestation. As a result, every exporter now needs to show exactly where each lot was grown. I strongly believe this is good news, because it rewards the farms that protect their forests.

THE ANSWER. Some farms are already changing. Shade-grown coffee protects the soil, and the trees keep the plants cooler during a dry season. Therefore, these farms often lose less of their crop in bad years. A certification also helps, because certified coffee usually earns a premium.

MY OPINION. Some people say that sustainability is only a cost. I am not convinced. A smaller carbon footprint leads to better relationships with buyers, and better prices lead to stronger farms. To be honest, the companies that ignore this will lose their customers. Sustainability is not a cost; it is the future of our business.

listenings.text: I work for a coffee cooperative in the south of Minas Gerais, and every week people ask me why our members are changing the way they farm. The answer is simple: the weather has changed. In the last five years, we have had two long droughts and one frost. Because of the dry seasons, our members lost a large part of their yield, and some families almost lost their farms. So we started a program with three steps. First, we plant trees between the coffee plants, because shade-grown coffee needs less water. Second, we help every smallholder to get a certification. As a result, they can sell to buyers who pay a premium. Third, we measure the water that each farm uses. It is not fast and it is not cheap, but in my view, it is the only way to keep these families on their land.

I buy green coffee for a roaster in Hamburg, and my customers have changed a lot. Ten years ago, they asked me only two questions: what is the price, and what is the quality. Today, the first question is often: where does this coffee come from, and how was it produced? The reason is the new European regulation on deforestation. Due to the new rules, I cannot buy a lot if the exporter cannot show me the exact farm. Some people in my company think that this is just more paperwork. Honestly, I am not convinced. I strongly believe that it is good for everyone. When an exporter can trace every bag, I trust the exporter more, and therefore I am happy to sign longer contracts. For me, a smaller carbon footprint and a clear origin are now part of the quality.

So the cooperative started to plant shade trees. Then it helped every farm to get a certification. Now its members earn a premium for certified coffee.
